events.event_narrative: Melting snow contributed to rising water levels on the Mattawamkeag River which eventually led to a prolonged interval of mostly lowland flooding along the river which began in late April. The flooding affected mostly the Bancroft Road between the towns of Wytopitlock and Danforth and several camps along the river. However...3.00 to 4.00 inches of rain fell across the region during late April...which along with continued snowmelt...enhanced the flooding. This enhanced flooding led to the evacuation of 15 homes in Mattawamkeag. This was a continuation of flooding which began in April. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Penobscot county from the late April and early May flooding.

A combination of 2.50 to 3.50 inches of rain which fell in late April and the melting of a record snowpack led to flooding along the Big Black River. The river crested nearly 2 feet above flood stage. The flooding affected mostly wilderness areas of the North Maine Woods bordering the river. This was a continuation of flooding which began in late April. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Aroostook county from the late April and early May flooding.

A combination of 2.50 to 3.50 inches of rain which fell in late April and the melting of a record snowpack led to flooding along the Saint Francis River. The river crested just under a foot above flood stage. The flooding affected mostly wilderness areas of the North Maine Woods bordering the river. This was a continuation of flooding which began in late April. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Aroostook county from the late April and early May flooding.

A combination of 2.50 to 3.50 inches of rain which fell in late April and the melting of a record snowpack led to historic flooding of the Saint John River at Fort Kent. The river crested at an all-time high level which was just over 5 feet above flood stage. The Fish River which flows into the Saint John River at Fort Kent also overflowed its banks...contributing to the Fort Kent flooding.|The Saint John River initially began flooding in the vicinity of the juncture with the Fish River when the waters of the Saint John River backed up into the Fish River. The initial flooding began with water running behind the levee which had been built along the Saint John River. Sandbagging efforts were eventually able to slow this flooding. However...with the Saint John River continuing to rise flooding expanded across the town. The river crested within a foot of the top of the levee which protects downtown Fort Kent. The levee did protect portions of downtown Fort Kent...though a significant portion of the town was flooded. The waters reached the base of the international bridge connecting Fort Kent with New Brunswick...causing closure of the bridge. There was concern for a time that the bridge might collapse...though the bridge did hold.|Between 100 and 150 homes were damaged or destroyed by the flooding in Fort Kent. Evacuations totaled between 600 and 1000 people. This was a continuation of flooding which began in late April. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Aroostook county from the late April and early May flooding.

A combination of 2.50 to 3.50 inches of rain which fell in late April and the melting of a record snowpack led to historic flooding of the Fish River at Fort Kent. The river crested at nearly 3 feet above flood stage. The flooding along the Fish River was enhanced due to water backing into it from the Saint John River which also crested at historic levels. The Fish River empties into the Saint John River at Fort Kent.|The initial flooding of the Fish River developed behind the levee which was built to protect Fort Kent from the Saint John River. Though sandbagging efforts were eventually able to help control the flooding of the Fish River...it still contributed to the inundation of portions of Fort Kent. This was a continuation of flooding which began in late April. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Aroostook county from the late April and early May flooding.

A combination of 2.00 to 3.00 inches of rain which fell in late April and the melting of a record snowpack led to flooding of the Aroostook River at Masardis. The river crested a little over 1 foot above flood stage. The flooding affected mostly lowland areas along the river and Route 11 near Masardis. This was a continuation of flooding which began in late April. The monetary damage represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Aroostook county from the late April and early May flooding.

A combination of 3.00 to 4.00 inches of rain which fell in late April and the melting of a record snowpack led to flooding along the East Branch of the Penobscot River at Grindstone. The river crested around 2 feet above flood stage. The flooding affected mostly lowland areas bordering the river along with portions of Route 11. This was a continuation of flooding which began in late April. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Penobscot county from the late April and early May flooding.

A combination of 3.00 to 4.00 inches of rain which fell in late April...the influx of water from tributary rivers and the melting of snow in headwater areas led to flooding of the Penobscot River at West Enfield. The river crested at slightly over 3.5 feet above flood stage. The flooding affected mostly lowland areas bordering the river. This was a continuation of flooding which began in late April. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Penobscot county from the late April and early May flooding.

A combination of 3.00 to 4.00 inches of rain which fell in late April and snowmelt in headwater areas led to flooding of the Piscataquis River at Medford. The river crested less than a half foot above flood stage. The flooding affected mostly lowland areas bordering the river. This was a continuation of flooding which began in late April. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Piscataquis county from the late April and early May flooding.

A combination of 2.00 to 3.50 inches of rain which fell in late April along with the melting of a record snowpack led to significant flooding across all of Aroostook county. All of the larger rivers across the county flooded to varying extents. The flooding on the Saint John River at Fort Kent and on the Fish River at Fort Kent both reached all-time historical levels. Many of the smaller rivers...streams and brooks also flooded to various extents.|Preliminary damage assessments indicated that nearly 400 homes across the county were impacted by flooding...which included around 200 homes with major damage and 14 homes which were destroyed. Some businesses were also damaged or destroyed. The most extensive damages occurred in the Fort Kent area.|Flooding was reported along the Saint John River from near Dickey to Van Buren. Portions of Route 161 were flooded and closed between Allagash and Fort Kent...isolating some towns for a time along western portions of Route 161. The Saint John River also flooded areas between Fort Kent and Van Buren. Some towns impacted by flooding along this portion of the Saint John River included Frenchville...Madawaska...Grand Isle...Keegan...Van Buren and Hamlin. Sections of both Route 1 and 1A were also flooded and closed in spots. Mandatory evacuations occurred in both Keegan and Van Buren. The international bridge crossing at Van Buren was closed due to damage to the Border Patrol Customs Office on the American side of the river. The international bridge crossing at Fort Kent was also closed for a time.|Flooding along the Fish River impacted portions of the towns of Soldier Pond and Wallagrass. Flooding along the Aroostook River occurred in the towns of Ashland...Washburn...Presque Isle and Fort Fairfield where the flooding affected mostly lowland areas bordering the river. Flooding along the West Branch of the Mattawamkeag River affected the town of Island Falls...while flooding along the East Branch of the Mattawamkeag River affected the town of Oakfield. In Houlton the Meduxnekeag River overflowed onto lowland areas bordering the river. Many other smaller rivers...streams and brooks also flooded which led to some road and bridge closures along with damage to infrastructure. At one point...a State of Emergency was declared for the entire county.|This was a continuation of flooding which began in late April. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Aroostook county from the late April and early May flooding.

A combination of 3.00 to 4.00 inches of rain which fell in late April along with the melting of a near record snowpack across northern portions of the county led to significant flooding across Penobscot county. The flooding initially began along smaller rivers and streams across northern portions of the county. These tributaries then flowed into the Penobscot River which flows south through the county. Flooding increased southward across the county as the flood crest moved south along the river.|Flooding was reported along the Penobscot River at Lincoln...Greenbush...Costigan...Milford...Old Town...West Enfield and Eddington. Much of the flooding along the Penobscot River affected mostly lowland areas bordering the river. However...some evacuations were needed at Milford. Smaller rivers...streams and brooks also flooded to varying extents across the county. Road flooding was reported in Newport...Palmyra...Corinna and Dexter. Roads...bridges...culverts and other infrastructure were damaged across the entire county.|This was a continuation of flooding which began in late April. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Penobscot county from the late April and early May flooding.

A combination of 3.00 to 4.00 inches of rain which fell in late April and the melting of a near record snowpack across northern portions of the county led to extensive flooding across all of Piscataquis county. Many rivers and streams overflowed their banks...producing varying degrees of flooding across the county. The flooding affected many towns...with many roads also flooded. Significant damage to public infrastructure was reported across the entire county.|Flooding was reported on the Piscataquis River at Dover-Foxcroft and on the Pleasant River at Brownville Junction. The flooding affected mostly lowland areas bordering the rivers. Other smaller rivers...streams and brooks also flooded. Several roads were flooded including Lakeview Plantation Road...Harlow Pond Road and the Back-Abbot Road.|This was a continuation of flooding which began in late April. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Piscataquis county from the late April and early May flooding.

The road closure was brief...only around 90 minutes...before the ice jam released allowing water levels to recede. The road was re-opened once river levels fell and ice was cleared from the road.

Northwest winds were sustained at 20 to 30 mph with gusts generally 35 to 45 mph. However...some gusts were in excess of 50 mph. The winds occurred from the early morning hours of the 24th into the afternoon. The winds toppled trees and snapped branches at scattered locations...with the most significant impacts across mostly eastern portions of the Saint John Valley including Fort Kent and Madawaska. Flash flooding developed during the early morning hours of the 15th around the Bangor/Brewer area. Numerous roads were closed and impassable due to the flash flooding. Some water rescues were also required...with standing water up to 4 feet deep in some locations. Several vehicles were also disabled due to the flash flood waters. Some roads and culverts in the area were damaged to varying extents. Rainfall totals with this event generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.50 inches...with local totals in excess of 5.00 inches.

Flash flooding developed during the early morning hours of the 15th. Several roads were impassable and closed due to the flash flooding. Road closures included Route 155 in Enfield along with Old Military Road near Winn. A portion of Old Military Road eventually collapsed due to flash flood waters overwhelming a culvert. Other roads and culverts were damaged to varying extents in the region. Rainfall totals with this event generally ranged from 2.00 to 4.00 inches...with local totals in excess of 4.00 inches.

The second heavy rain event in 4 days led to flooding which contributed to a train derailment. The first heavy rain event from the 14th into the 15th produced general 2.50 to 4.50 inch rain totals. This left the ground saturated and water levels elevated. A second heavy rain event from the 18th into the 19th produced an additional 2.00 to 3.00 inches of rain. Flooding developed during the early morning hours of the 19th. The flooding overwhelmed a culvert located beneath a rail bed. Failure of the culvert led to a washout and collapse of the rail bed leaving the tracks unsupported. The unsupported tracks contributed to a train derailment during the early morning hours of the 19th. The first seven cars of a train derailed while crossing the unsupported tracks. No injuries occurred. The time of the initial washout is estimated.

Sustained winds of 25 to 35 mph...with gusts to around 60 mph...occurred during the early morning hours of the 1st. A wind gust of 61 mph was measured at Sedgwick Ridge. Wind gusts of 58 mph were measured at both Castine and near Brooksville. The winds brought down branches and toppled or snapped trees which contributed to power outages. Some roads were also blocked by fallen trees. Blocked roads were reported near Somesville and Blue Hill. A vehicle struck a tree across the road near Ellsworth. Other trees were reported down near Sorrento and on Deer Isle.

Heavy rain...with totals of 2.00 to 3.00 inches...produced localized flooding across portions of southern Piscataquis county. Several roads in low lying areas around the town of Abbot were flooded...along with Back Road in Abbot...leading to road closures. The mainstem of the Piscataquis River in Dover-Foxcroft crested around a half foot above flood stage during the evening of the 1st. The river then fell back below flood stage during the early morning hours of the 2nd.

A combination of 3.00 to 4.00 inches of rain which fell in late April...the influx of water from tributary rivers and the melting of snow in headwater areas led to flooding of the Penobscot River at Eddington. The river crested at around 1.50 feet above flood stage. The flooding affected mostly lowland areas bordering the river. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Penobscot county from the late April and early May flooding.

Heavy rains then occurred through the remainder of the morning into the afternoon...with lighter rains then persisting into the early morning hours of the 19th. Numerous road closures occurred countywide. Extensive flooding occurred along the mainstem Piscataquis River. Flooding developed through the afternoon and evening of the 18th. Locations along the river generally crested through the morning and afternoon of the 19th...falling back below flood stage that evening. At Dover-Foxcroft the river crested at 16.77 feet, around 6 feet above flood stage...the highest level in decades. The crest at Medford was 13.55 feet, around a half foot above flood stage. An all time record flood stage was set at Blanchard at 13.4 feet, around 3 feet above flood stage. The previous record was 11.4 feet. Flooding along the Piscataquis river impacted roads...bridges...some buildings including residences and other infrastructure.

The crest at Eddington was around flood stage. At Grindstone...on the East Branch of the Penobscot River...the river crested at 14.7 feet, nearly 2 feet above flood stage. Flooding along the Penobscot River impacted roads...bridges...some buildings and other infrastructure.

In Bar Harbor, the NOAA water level gauge observed 15.7 feet MLLW, briefly setting a record that was surpassed by the January 13th, 2024 event.

The dike at Machias became overtopped and water flooded Court street in downtown Machias, inundating several buildings. In Roque Bluffs, the state park received extensive erosion and Johnson Cover road was inundated, stranding several residents. The tide gauge at Cutler Farris Wharf reached 18.56 feet, just below minor flood stage.

Storm drains were quickly overwhelmed and streams quickly overflowed. Water depths of 3 to 4 feet were reported in some low lying areas of Blue Hill submerging vehicles and flooding some buildings. An ice jam on the Saint John River at Nine Mile Bridge caused minor flooding. The river crested around a foot above flood stage. The flooding affected wilderness areas of the North Maine Woods bordering the river.

An ice jam on the Aroostook River at Washburn caused brief flooding. River levels rose quickly behind the ice jam...cresting around 2.5 feet above flood stage. The ice jam persisted for just over an hour before releasing. River levels quickly fell with the release of the ice jam.

The flooding affected mostly lowland areas along the river. However...the flooding did lead to the closure of Route 11. Several homes were also affected by the flooding. One home had water filling the basement...while a second home had around 2 feet of water on the first floor.

A combination of ice jams...rain and run-off from melting snow contributed to flooding across Aroostook county. Many rivers and streams overflowed their banks...producing various degrees of flooding across the county. The flooding affected several towns and led to some road closures. Most of the flooding was minor...generally affecting lowland areas bordering the rivers and streams.|In the Fort Fairfield area an ice jam developed during the morning of the 6th in the vicinity of the bridge crossing the Aroostook River. The ice moved toward Tinker Dam that afternoon then re-jammed causing fluctuating river levels. The ice jam persisted near Tinker Dam through much of the 7th keeping river levels elevated. The ice jam released during the evening of the 7th...with river levels dropping rapidly with the release of the ice jam.  |A persistent ice jam on the Aroostook River between Washburn and Crouseville caused elevated river levels which flooded portions of Route 164 to depths of 1 to 2 feet in spots keeping the road closed for 4 days. A mini-supercell thunderstorm produced an EF1 tornado at the town of Eagle Lake. The tornado began near the Pinette Brook crossing of Convent Road. The tornado was then intermittently on the ground while moving through  Eagle Lake...eventually dissipating just before crossing State Route 11. Along the tornado path...hundreds of trees were snapped or uprooted in intermittent swaths and patches (DI 27, DOD 4). The tornado also destroyed an outbuilding...moderately damaged one home and caused minor damage to several homes and vehicles. A transport trailer was also overturned. Based on the damage...the tornado winds were estimated at around 110 mph. The average path width was around 150 yards.

High surf generated from Hurricane Bill...which was tracking well east of the region...produced large waves along the Maine coast. A large wave washed a group of spectators at Thunder Hole...in Acadia National Park...into the ocean. The spectators had gathered to watch the high surf break along the rocky coast. The wave washed 7 individuals into the water...4 of which were able to exit the water on their own. Of the remaining 3...2 were rescued by the Coast Guard. The final individual...a 7 year old girl...perished before she could be rescued. The girl was in the water for over 3 hours before her body was recovered. In addition to the fatality...13 individuals were injured when the same wave slammed people on to rocks. The injuries varied in severity...ranging from broken and dislocated bones to lacerations. Some of the injured had to be transported to the hospital...while others transported themselves.

River and stream levels across the region then stabilized and began to fall during the morning of the 27th.

Tropical Storm Earl tracked east of the region during the early morning hours of the 4th...eventually making landfall on the east coast of Nova Scotia mid morning. The|minimum surface pressure across the region was 989 mb. Sustained winds of 15 to 25 mph...with gusts of 30 to 40 mph...occurred along the immediate Downeast coast during the early morning hours of the 4th. A peak gust of 35 mph was reported at Prospect Harbor. There were no reports of wind related damage. Storm surge was not a factor.|The storm also brought heavy rain. Rainfall totals of 1.50 to 3.00 inches were common across much of the region...with localized totals of 4.00 to 5.00 inches. Thus...although the heavy rain caused elevated water levels on brooks and rivers...no flooding was reported.

An EF0 tornado snapped or uprooted numerous trees along an intermittent path. The tornado initially touched down around 1 mile east-southeast of Little Madawaska Lake. The tornado was embedded within an area of damaging straight line winds...intermittently touching down along its path. The final touch down point was around 4 miles west-northwest of Loring Air Force Base. Most of the damage along the path was uprooted or snapped trees. However...the tornado destroyed an older barn (DI 1, DOD 5) and damaged several farm outbuildings on the Brissette Road. Several other outbuildings were damaged or destroyed at various points along the path. Several homes (DI 2, DOD 2) received damage to shingles and siding. Damage along the path was due to a combination of straight line winds and the intermittent tornado touchdowns.

A nearly stationary thunderstorm produced 6.00 to 8.00 inches of rain in less than 4 hours in Brownville. These very heavy rains produced severe flash flooding from Brownville to Milo. Numerous roads in the Brownville and Milo areas were heavily damaged or completely washed away along with several bridges resulting in road closures. Roads heavily damaged or washed out in spots around Brownville included Route 11...Church Street...High Street...Main Road...Pleasant River Road...Quarry Road...Barnard Road...Stickney Hill Road and Lakeview Road. Gullies on some roads were 5 to 10 feet deep and 20 to 30 feet wide. A nearly 200 yard stretch of Stickney Hill was washed on to Stickney Hill Road. Damage to roads was so extensive that the town of Brownville was nearly isolated for several hours. A parking lot along Route 11 was completely washed away. The railroad tracks around Brownville were undercut and damaged in several locations. Homes...businesses and vehicles in Brownvile were flooded. Significant damage occurred to the infrastructure around Brownville with the entire town losing power. Water rescues were required for several individuals at the height of the flooding. Flooding was also reported around Milo with several roads damaged and closed. Basement flooding was also extensive in Milo. A motorist was killed (indirect fatality) around 5 AM Sunday morning when his car crashed into a gully...5 feet deep and 20 to 30 feet wide...which had been cut into the Pleasant River Road by the flash flooding. The driver was killed from the impact of the accident and not drowning.

Mild temperatures of around 60 to the mid 60s caused rapid snow melt and runoff during the 14th which led to rising river and stream levels. Heavy rain then occurred during the 15th in advance of a slow moving cold front along with continued mild temperatures which contributed to further runoff. Rainfall totals during the 15th generally ranged from 1.00 to 2.00 inches. |Flooding began to develop during the afternoon of the 15th due to rising river and stream levels along with ice jams. Additional flooding was due to runoff from fields and hills which overwhelmed culverts and produced standing water in poor drainage areas. Road closures due to both types of flooding began to develop during the afternoon of the 15th. The number of road closures then steadily increased across the entire county through the remainder of the 15th into the 16th...with numerous road closures persisting into the 18th. |Flooding occurred along portions of both the Aroostook River and Saint John River. Numerous roads were closed around Fort Fairfield...on the Aroostook River...starting on the afternoon of the 15th due to elevated river levels and several ice jams. The final ice jams released during the afternoon of the 16th allowing water levels to recede.  Several forecast points along the Aroostook River reached flood stage. An ice jam caused the river at Washburn to briefly spike above flood stage for around 2 hours during the overnight hours of the 15th into the 16th...cresting around 2.5 feet above flood stage. At Masardis...the river rose above flood stage during the early morning hours of the 16th...crested around a foot above flood stage that afternoon...then fell below flood stage later that evening. Elevated river levels and ice jams contributed to flooding along portions of the Saint John River. An ice jam affected the Saint Francis area during the morning of the 16th resulting in minor flooding. A more significant ice jam...estimated to be 3 to 4 miles long...then affected the Saint Francis area during the 17th into the early morning of the 18th before releasing. This ice jam closed portions of Route 161 between Saint Francis and Allagash due to water and large chunks of ice covering the road. This ice jam also caused the voluntary evacuation of 5 homes along the river for precautionary reasons. When this ice jam released the ice contributed to elevated river levels further downstream...from Hamlin to Van Buren...where portions of Route 1A were briefly closed. Many small streams also overflowed across the county contributing to flooding. Other towns affected by flooding and road closures included Bridgewater...Caribou...Castle Hill...Easton...Hodgdon...Houlton...Mapleton...Presque Isle...Westfield and Wytopitlock.  |Non river flooding also occurred across the region due to the runoff of heavy rain and snow melt from fields and hills. This runoff overwhelmed culverts which led to flooding and road closures...with flooding also occurring in poor drainage areas. The one fatality during this event was due to runoff from fields which had flooded a dirt road in the Caswell area. After moving his vehicle...the individual attempted to walk back across the flooded road and stepped into the fast moving water of a culvert which swept him away resulting in his drowning. This fatality occurred during the evening of the 15th. The monetary damage represents a total from 4 towns. Most of this damage was related to flooding from fields.

Runoff from heavy rain and melting snow contributed to flooding and several road closures. Flooding began to develop during the evening of the 15th...lasting into the afternoon of the 17th. Road closures included Route 6 near Lambert Lake and portions of Route 169 between Danforth and Springfield.

Flooding due to runoff from heavy rain and snow melt...along with ice jams...began to develop during the evening of the 15th. Flooding then persisted into the afternoon of the 17th. The Dover-Foxcroft forecast point on the Piscataquis River rose above flood stage during the early morning hours of the 16th...crested almost 2 feet above flood stage later that morning...then fell back below flood stage later that evening. Road closures were reported in the towns of Abbot...Brownville...Greenville...Milo...Sangerville and Willamantic. A bridge over the Sebec River...in the town of Sebec...was closed. A bridge over the Piscataquis River in Sangerville was also closed. Flooding was also reported along portions of the Pleasant River. The monetary damages are from 2 towns.

Flooding due to runoff from heavy rain and snow melt...along with ice jams...began to develop during the evening of the 15th then persisted into the early morning hours of the 18th. |In Dexter...a culvert collapsed during the morning of the 16th causing flooding and road closures along Center Street...Main Street and Lincoln Street. The Lincoln Street bridge was also closed due to significant damage to the road. Additional flooding occurred in Dexter during the morning of the 17th when the East Branch of the Sebasticook River overflowed its banks. This flooding led to evacuations along Lincoln Street...Liberty Street and Water Street.|Flooding occurred at several forecast points along the Penobscot River. At West Enfield the river rose above flood stage during the afternoon of the 16th...crested just under a foot above flood stage later that afternoon...then fell back below flood stage during the evening of the 17th. At Eddington the river briefly rose barely above flood stage during the early morning hours of the 18th. An ice jam on the East Branch of the Penobscot River during the afternoon of the 16th caused flooding which closed Route 11 between Grindstone and Soldierton. Route 2 near Greenbush was closed due to flooding during the morning of the 17th. The Kenduskeag Plaza in downtown Bangor was also flooded when the Kenduskeag Stream overflowed. Additional flooding and road closures were reported in the towns of Dexter and Lincoln.

events.event_narrative: Locally gusty winds up to 30 mph briefly occurred along the leading edge of an area of rain moving along the Downeast coast near Schoodic Point. Three sea kayakers encountered the gusty winds in an area of dangerous currents. The combination of gusty winds and dangerous currents caused the kayaks to overturn and spill the occupants...2 men and a woman...into the water. The dangerous currents and tides then drew the kayakers further offshore. The two male kayakers perished from a combination of hypothermia and drowning (indirect). The female kayaker was rescued and hospitalized but survived (indirect).  The wind gusts and time of the event are estimated.

events.event_narrative: Wind gusts were estimated at up to 52 knots with a severe thunderstorm crossing Deer Isle. The wind gusts brought down powerlines on the island.

A severe thunderstorm produced a microburst which developed around Castle Hill and persisted through Crouseville and Washburn before ending in southwest Caribou. Around three dozen trees were snapped or toppled near Castle Hill...where some outdoor equipment was also damaged or destroyed. Tree damage was also observed in the Crouseville and Washburn areas. The metal roof of a barn was damaged in southwest Caribou before the microburst ended near Bailey Road. Maximum wind gusts with the microburst were estimated at 90 to 100 mph. The path length of the microburst was around 7 miles. The maximum path width was around 1 mile.

A severe thunderstorm produced a microburst in the Limestone area. One barn was completely destroyed. Another barn has its roof torn off. Large trees were also snapped or toppled along the nearly 5 mile path of the microburst which ended aboubt a half mile north of Limestone. One uprooted tree fell on to the roof of a house. Maximum wind speeds with the microburst were estimated at 100 to 110 mph. The maximum path width was around a half mile.
Several trees were toppled by wind gusts estimated at up to 60 mph. The time is estimated.

Melting snow contributed to rising levels on the Mattawamkeag River which eventually led to a prolonged interval of mostly lowland flooding along the river. This flooding affected mostly the Bancroft Road between the towns of Wytopitlock and Danforth and several camps along the river. However...3.00 to 4.00 inches of rain fell across the region toward the end of the month...along with continued snow melt...which enhanced the flooding. The late month flooding led to the evacuation of 15 homes in Mattawamkeag. The flooding continued into May. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure for all of Penobscot county. In this instance the damage occurred late in the month.

An ice jam on the Aroostook River near Washburn caused brief minor flooding. The flooding lasted less than an hour...with water levels rising less than a half foot above flood stage. River levels quickly fell with the release of the ice jam.

An ice jam on the Saint John River near Dickey contributed to several hours of flooding. At its maximum level...the river reached nearly 4 feet above flood stage. A portion of Route 161 was closed for a time during the flooding when water covered the road. River levels quickly fell with the release of the ice jam.

A combination of 2.50 to 3.50 inches of rain and the melting of a record snowpack led to flooding along the Big Black River. The river crested nearly 2 feet above flood stage. The flooding affected mostly wilderness areas of the North Maine Woods bordering the river. The flooding continued into May. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Aroostook county.

A combination of 2.50 to 3.50 inches of rain and the melting of a record snowpack led to historic flooding of the Saint John River at Fort Kent. The river crested at an all-time high level which was just over 5 feet above flood stage. The Fish River which flows into the Saint John River at Fort Kent also overflowed its banks...contributing to the Fort Kent flooding. |The Saint John River initially began flooding in the vicinity of the juncture with the Fish River when the waters of the Saint John River backed up into the Fish River. The initial flooding began with water running behind the levee which had been built along the Saint John River. Sandbagging efforts were eventually able to slow this flooding. However...with the Saint John River continuing to rise flooding expanded across the town. The river crested within a foot of the top of the levee which protects downtown Fort Kent. The levee did protect portions of downtown Fort Kent...though a significant portion of the town was flooded. The waters reached the base of the international bridge connecting Fort Kent with New Brunswick...causing closure of the bridge. There was concern for a time that the bridge might collapse...though the bridge did hold. |Between 100 and 150 homes were damaged or destroyed by the flooding in Fort Kent. Evacuations totaled between 600 and 1000 people. The flooding continued into May. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Aroostook county.

A combination of 2.00 to 3.50 inches of rain along with the melting of a record snowpack contributed to significant flooding across all of Aroostook county. All of the larger rivers across the county flooded to various extents. The flooding on the Saint John River at Fort Kent and on the Fish River at Fort Kent both reached all-time historical levels. Many of the smaller rivers...streams and brooks also flooded to various extents.|Preliminary damage assessments indicated that nearly 400 homes across the county were impacted by flooding...which included around 200 homes with major damage and 14 homes which were destroyed. Some businesses were also damaged or destroyed. The most extensive damages occurred in the Fort Kent area. |Flooding was reported along the Saint John River from near Dickey to Van Buren. Portions of Route 161 were flooded and closed between Allagash and Fort Kent...isolating some towns for a time along western portions of Route 161. The Saint John River also flooded areas between Fort Kent and Van Buren. Some towns flooded along this portion of the Saint John River included Frenchville...Madawaska...Grand Isle...Keegan...Van Buren and Hamlin. Sections of Route 1 and 1A were flooded and closed in spots. Mandatory evacuations occurred in both Keegan and Van Buren. The international bridge crossing at Van Buren was closed due to damage to the Border Patrol Customs office on the American side of the river. The international bridge crossing at Fort Kent was also closed for a time.|Flooding along the Fish River impacted portions of the towns of Soldier Pond and Wallagrass. Flooding on the Aroostook River occurred in the towns of Ashland...Washburn...Presque Isle and Fort Fairfield where the flooding affected mostly lowland areas bordering the river. Flooding along the West Branch of the Mattawamkeag River affected Island Falls...while flooding along the East Branch of the Mattawamkeag River affected Oakfield. In Houlton the Meduxnekeag River overflowed onto lowland areas bordering the river.|Many other smaller streams and brooks also flooded...leading to some road and bridge closures and damage to infrastructure. A State of Emergency was declared for the entire county.|Flooding across the county continued into May. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across the entire county.

A combination of 3.00 to 4.00 inches of rain along with the melting of a near record snowpack across northern portions of the county contributed to significant flooding across the county. The flooding initially began along smaller rivers and streams across northern portions of the county. These tributaries then flowed into the Penobscot River which flows south through the county. Flooding increased southward across the county as the flood crest moved south along the Penobscot River.|Flooding was reported along the Penobscot river at Lincoln...Greenbush...Costigan...Milford...Old Town...West Enfield and Eddington.|Much of the flooding along the Penobscot river affected mostly lowland areas bordering the river. However...some evacuations were needed at Milford.|Smaller rivers and streams also flooded to varying extents across the county. Road flooding was reported in the towns of Newport...Palmyra...Corinna and Dexter.|Roads...bridges...culverts and other public infrastucture were damaged across the entire county. The flooding continued into May. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Penobscot county.

A combination of 3.00 to 4.00 inches of rain and the melting of a near record snowpack across northern portions of the county led to extensive flooding across all of Piscataquis county. Many rivers and streams overflowed their banks...producing various degrees of flooding across the county. The flooding affected many towns...with many roads also flooded. Significant damage to public infrastructure was reported across the entire county.|Flooding was reported on the Piscataquis River at Dover-Foxcroft and on the Pleasant River at Brownville Junction. The flooding affected mostly lowland areas bordering the rivers. Other smaller rivers and streams also overflowed. Several roads were flooded including Lakeview Plantation Road...Harlow Pond Road and Back-Abbot Road. The flooding continued into May. The monetary value represents the total damage to public infrastructure across all of Piscataquis county.
